"executive_summary": "This paper reports a continuous flow protocol for the organophotoredox-catalysed radical cation [2+2]-cycloaddition (dimerization) of electron-rich alkenes, namely vinyl carbazoles and styrenes, to give cyclobutane dimers. The authors merge homogeneous small-molecule organophotoredox catalysis with a commercial continuous flow platform to address limitations of prior batch methods, which required cryogenic temperatures, excessive reaction times, and higher catalyst loadings. Using a pyrillium organophotoredox catalyst (10), the target carbazole host material 1,2-transdicarbazylcyclobutane (t-DCzCB, 1) was synthesized in 82% isolated yield under batch conditions, but in up to 93% yield under optimized continuous flow conditions at 0.5 mL.min⁻¹ (τ = 20 min), 2 mol% catalyst, and 450 nm irradiation. Flow conditions also enabled greatly reduced catalyst loadings (down to 0.1 mol% at 10 mmol scale, giving 79% yield) and shorter reaction times. The scope was expanded to brominated, chloro-, methoxy-, hydroxy-, and aryl-substituted vinyl carbazoles, as well as styrenes, including the natural lignan magnosalin (4) on a 10 mmol scale (40% yield). The work demonstrates that continuous flow improves yields, reduces catalyst loading, and shortens reaction times relative to batch chemistry, providing scalable routes to functional cyclobutane materials and natural products. The study is notable for using a commercial off-the-shelf flow platform and for mechanistic probes of reversibility and background oxidation. However, several details are limited: the catalyst structure is not fully specified, reaction times for some substrates (e.g., 5 days for 12a in batch) are reported qualitatively, and the bibliography is absent, so top_influential_citations must be set to \"\". summary.title: Dimeric cyclobutane formation under continuous flow conditions using organophotoredox catalysed [2+2]-cycloaddition
summary.authors: Helena F Grantham; Marc C Kimber; M F C Grantham; Kimber
summary.executive_summary: This paper reports a continuous flow protocol for the organophotoredox-catalysed radical cation [2+2]-cycloaddition (dimerization) of electron-rich alkenes, namely vinyl carbazoles and styrenes, to give cyclobutane dimers. The authors merge homogeneous small-molecule organophotoredox catalysis with a commercial continuous flow platform to address limitations of prior batch methods, which required cryogenic temperatures, excessive reaction times, and higher catalyst loadings. Using a pyrillium organophotoredox catalyst (10), the target carbazole host material 1,2-transdicarbazylcyclobutane (t-DCzCB, 1) was synthesized in 82% isolated yield under batch conditions, but in up to 93% yield under optimized continuous flow conditions at 0.5 mL.min⁻¹ (τ = 20 min), 2 mol% catalyst, and 450 nm irradiation. Flow conditions also enabled greatly reduced catalyst loadings (down to 0.1 mol% at 10 mmol scale, giving 79% yield) and shorter reaction times. The scope was expanded to brominated, chloro-, methoxy-, hydroxy-, and aryl-substituted vinyl carbazoles, as well as styrenes, including the natural lignan magnosalin (4) on a 10 mmol scale (40% yield). The work demonstrates that continuous flow improves yields, reduces catalyst loading, and shortens reaction times relative to batch chemistry, providing scalable routes to functional cyclobutane materials and natural products. The study is notable for using a commercial off-the-shelf flow platform and for mechanistic probes of reversibility and background oxidation. However, several details are limited: the catalyst structure is not fully specified, reaction times for some substrates (e.g., 5 days for 12a in batch) are reported qualitatively, and the bibliography is absent, so top_influential_citations must be set to "". Data/code and ethics fields are also unreported and set to "". The paper is a synthetic methodology report rather than a computational or data-driven study, so reproducibility rests on the described conditions and yields rather than deposited datasets.

However, several details are limited: the catalyst structure is not fully specified, reaction times for some substrates (e.g., 5 days for 12a in batch) are reported qualitatively, and the bibliography is absent, so top_influential_citations must be set to "". Data/code and ethics fields are also unreported and set to "". The paper is a synthetic methodology report rather than a computational or data-driven study, so reproducibility rests on the described conditions and yields rather than deposited datasets.

Research Context
Cyclobutane dimers are valuable functional materials and natural products. Electron-rich alkenes dimerize via radical cation [2+2]-cycloaddition. Vinyl carbazole is a precursor to the electrophosphorescence host t-DCzCB. Styrenes such as E-asarone are precursors to the lignan magnosalin. Organophotoredox catalysis offers advantages over metal-based catalysts. Prior organophotoredox dimerizations had practical limitations. Continuous flow improves irradiation and conversion in photoredox reactions.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The study asks whether continuous flow improves organophotoredox dimerization. The hypothesis is that flow gives higher yields and shorter times. The hypothesis is that flow allows lower catalyst loadings. The hypothesis is that flow enables functionalized and natural product synthesis. The predicted outcome is that flow outperforms batch across substrates.

Methodological Details
The study compares continuous flow versus batch conditions. A commercial off-the-shelf continuous flow platform was used. The pyrillium organophotoredox catalyst is denoted 10. The target carbazole host material is t-DCzCB (1). Batch synthesis used 3 mol% catalyst under Nicewicz conditions. Batch synthesis gave 82% isolated yield of t-DCzCB. Batch required deoxygenated acetone, cryogenic temperatures, and extended times. Yields were analyzed by HPLC using p-terphenyl as internal standard. HPLC required calibration of 2 and 1. Full HPLC details are in the supporting information. The reaction was run at 1.00 mmol of 2 at 0.4 M in acetone. Optimal flow conditions: 0.5 mL.min⁻¹, τ = 20 min, 2 mol%, 450 nm. Optimal continuous flow yield was 93% at 1 mol% catalyst. Substrates were vinyl carbazoles 12a-24a, made by the Obora method. Vinyl carbazoles were made in moderate to good yields. 1-bromo-9-vinylcarbazole (15a) was isolated in very low yields. Natural product magnosalin (4) was the styrene lignan target.

Procedures And Architectures
The mechanism is radical cation formation, cycloaddition, and reduction. The cyclobutyl radical cation is reduced to the dimer. Irradiation was performed at 450 nm. An alternative wavelength of 405 nm was tested. An alternative wavelength of 420 nm was tested. The reaction did not proceed without catalyst. The reaction did not proceed without irradiation. Flow rate was lowered from 5 to 2 mL.min⁻¹ to test reversibility. A 10 mmol scale run used 0.1 mol% catalyst. Substrates were made by Suzuki coupling and vinylation. Brominated products were made via Suzuki coupling of 13b. Borylation used bis(pinacolato)diboron to make 26. An electron relay anthracene was added to the styrene solution. Diethylaniline was used as an electron relay for styrene 29. E-asarone dimerization used anthracene as an electron relay. The lignan magnosalin was made on a 10 mmol scale.

Key Results
Optimal flow yield of t-DCzCB was 93% at 1 mol% catalyst. A 4.5 mol% catalyst loading gave 90% yield. Lowering flow to 2 mL.min⁻¹ reduced yield to 79%. A 10 mmol scale run at 0.1 mol% gave 79% yield. Reducing flow to 0.1 mL.min⁻¹ dropped yield to 53%. Carbazole formed as a byproduct at low flow rate. 405 nm and 420 nm gave comparable yields to 450 nm. The reaction failed without catalyst or light. Batch dimerization of 12a gave 48% yield. Flow dimerization of 12a gave 64% yield in 50 min. Batch dimerization of 13a gave 31% yield. Flow dimerization of 13a gave 71% yield. Flow dimerization of 16a gave 65% yield. Batch slightly outperformed flow for 17a. Flow gave 61% for 18b and 45% for 19b. Flow gave 25% for the bis-enol ether 21b. Flow gave 65% for the fluoroarylated cyclobutane 22b. Flow gave 57% for the tetra-alkyl dimer 23b. Flow gave 50% for the bisarylated cyclobutane 24b. Flow gave 44% for the styrene dimer 28. Flow gave 22% for pellucidin A (29). Flow gave 40% for magnosalin (4) on 10 mmol scale. Suzuki coupling of 13b gave cyclobutane 25 in 75% yield. Borylation gave 26 in 36% yield. 1-bromo-9-vinylcarbazole (15a) gave no cyclobutane product.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
Flow improves yields and reduces catalyst loading versus batch. Lower flow rates indicate possible reversibility of the dimerization. Carbazole byproduct arises from background oxygen oxidation. The mechanism requires both catalyst and light. Flow enables functionalized carbazole dimers. Flow enables scalable synthesis of the lignan magnosalin. The protocol is general, robust, and scalable. Flow reduces reaction times versus batch.

Contradictions And Limitations
Batch slightly outperformed flow for substrate 17a. 1-bromo-9-vinylcarbazole gave no cyclobutane product. The catalyst structure is not fully specified in the text. Reaction times for some substrates are reported qualitatively. Solubility at 0.4 M was challenging, requiring 0.2 M. The exact flow platform model is not specified.

Claims
Continuous flow improves organophotoredox dimerization yields, reduces catalyst loading, and shortens reaction times versus batch. Optimal flow yield of t-DCzCB was 93% at 1 mol% catalyst. A 10 mmol scale run at 0.1 mol% gave 79% yield. Flow gave 71% for 13b versus 31% batch. Flow gave 64% for 12b versus 48% batch. The protocol is general, robust, and scalable. Batch slightly outperformed flow for substrate 17a. 1-bromo-9-vinylcarbazole gave no cyclobutane product. The protocol enables scalable synthesis of functional materials. The protocol enables scalable synthesis of the lignan magnosalin.
The dimerization is reversible and sensitive to oxygen, as evidenced by yield loss at low flow rates and carbazole byproduct formation. Lowering flow to 2 mL.min⁻¹ reduced yield to 79%. Reducing flow to 0.1 mL.min⁻¹ dropped yield to 53%. Carbazole formed as a byproduct at low flow rate. The reaction failed without catalyst or light. 405 nm and 420 nm gave comparable yields to 450 nm. Optimized flow conditions minimize reversibility and oxygen exposure.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The reaction failed without catalyst. The reaction failed without irradiation. Alternative wavelengths gave comparable yields. A 10 mmol scale run at 0.1 mol% gave 79% yield.

Key Figures Tables
Table 1 is the optimization study of the continuous flow synthesis. Scheme 1 shows cyclobutane dimers as functional materials and natural products. Scheme 2 shows the radical cation [2+2]-cycloaddition mechanism. Scheme 3 shows the merged organophotoredox and flow protocol. Scheme 4 shows the batch versus flow comparison for t-DCzCB. Scheme 5 shows the substrate scope of brominated carbazoles. Scheme 6 shows the synthetic potential of bromocyclobutane products. Scheme 7 shows the styrene and lignan dimerizations.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is a continuous flow organophotoredox dimerization protocol. 2. The strongest evidence is the 93% flow yield versus 82% batch yield for t-DCzCB. 3. The future path is scalable synthesis of functional materials and natural products.
